disagreements.issue: Appropriate funding source for Cashers Valley Road sewer extension ($88,400 commitment)

positions.position: Opposed using Rosenwald fund ($25,000) as proposed source; advocated for finding alternative from maintenance budget with larger balance; expressed concern about impact on Rosenwald area road/sidewalk improvements and Silverstein Park bathroom funding

Cautioned that maintenance budget line item is already allocated to non-revenue water efforts and new trucks; moving funds risks those priorities; acknowledged support for project but concerned about funding source trade-offs

Emphasized the 11th-hour nature of $88,000 request (quotes came in within weeks); stressed importance of knowing funding sources in advance given tight budgets; requested that council revisit decision in two weeks after examining all options with full information

Proposed three funding sources (water/sewer capital reserve, Rosenwald fund, water/sewer operating); stated willingness to present alternative options in two weeks but initially defended proposed combination; explained quotes came in late

disagreements.issue: Framing of loitering/disruptive behavior ordinance as homelessness issue vs. broader community quality-of-life issue

positions.position: Argued ordinances disproportionately impact unhoused population; warned of creating criminal barriers to housing eligibility; advocated for working with service providers and existing plans rather than criminalization

Argued that ignoring disruptive behavior enables bad habits; emphasized personal responsibility and law enforcement as compassionate measure; cited tourism and business impacts; warned of community decline without enforcement

Pushed back against framing as homelessness issue; noted that data shows 52% of calls involve non-unhoused individuals; emphasized this is community-wide problem, not exclusive to unhoused population; stated preference not to fall into narrative trap

Acknowledged difficulty of balancing policy; explicitly rejected 'cruelty as policy' approach; emphasized that seeing unhoused person doesn't mean witnessing crime; called for mental health resources from state/federal government; reaffirmed commitment to safe housing as city goal; acknowledged behavioral health crisis requires resources beyond city capacity

Echoed baker's concern about balancing enforcement and support; emphasized need to tackle 'crisis from all ends' including law enforcement ability to act plus downstream social services and housing; committed to seriousness about underlying crisis

disagreements.issue: Legal interpretation of 'loitering' language and officer enforcement discretion

positions.position: Concerned that 'habitually loaf or loiter on the streets' is too vague and creates liability for officers; proposed amendment to make second clause ('obstruct or interfere with free passage') apply to first clause, or strike first part entirely to require actual obstruction for violation

Interpreted ordinance as two separate and independent clauses connected by comma: (1) habitually loaf/loiter, and (2) congregate to obstruct/interfere; noted this has been on books for long time; only penalty is changing; noted that any amendment to remove vagueness would be political decision

Acknowledged discretion challenge; stated that 'loitering' might apply to single person intentionally obstructing passage, while 'congregating' would apply to multiple people; indicated officer judgment varies by specific situation; acknowledged amendment might be 'fair enough' to improve enforceability and reduce liability

Moved amended language: remove 'loitering generally' from section title; amend section 42-5(C) to read 'It shall be unlawful to loiter or congregate on the streets or sidewalks of the city in such a way as to obstruct or interfere with free passage into or out of any public business or private property' - making obstruction requirement apply to both loitering and congregating

public_comment.summary: Urged caution on ordinances that would criminalize conduct already covered by state law. public_comment.speaker: Doug Powell
public_comment.summary: Argued that living on streets is not normal and communities should enforce laws to discourage this lifestyle as compassionate measure. Cited personal experience in another community addressing homelessness through business impact assessment. Recounted cautionary tale of Ventura, California's decline due to inadequate law enforcement response to disruptive behavior, culminating in random violence (stabbing death). Warned that ignoring enforcement issues while investing in tourism puts Brevard at risk of similar transformation.
public_comment.topic: Law enforcement and quality of life; homelessness as unsustainable; cautionary example from Ventura, California

public_comment.speaker: James Beal
public_comment.summary: Expressed appreciation for Bracken Trail and its developer while raising concerns about unintended consequences. Stated that nine properties on Pinnacle Road (formerly Mackie Ridge Road) are adversely affected because vehicle access was eliminated after trail construction. Residents can no longer drive to purchase groceries and return to unload. Claimed the city 'did something wrong' in eminent domain process and urged deeper investigation, stating council is uniquely positioned to solve problem.
public_comment.topic: Bracken Trail property access issues and city's eminent domain process

public_comment.speaker: Adam Perkins
public_comment.summary: Requested that MSD task force include Heart of Brevard organization given 30-year partnership and 4-year contract administration experience. Proposed two-phase process: Phase 1 (defining downtown needs and scope) should include Heart of Brevard's executive director or another executive committee member; Phase 2 (bid review/scoring) could maintain distance for conflict-of-interest concerns. Noted that North Carolina Main Street program confirmed involvement in Phase 1 is standard best practice and not a conflict. If direct representation excluded, requested ability to appoint representative from partner organization (tourism authority or downtown property owner).
public_comment.topic: Municipal Service District (MSD) task force composition and Heart of Brevard representation

public_comment.speaker: Doug Powell
public_comment.summary: Powell spoke on compassion and fairness regarding homelessness. Based on his ministry experience, he argued homelessness is a symptom of underlying addiction and mental health issues, not primarily a housing issue. He expressed concern that subsidizing homeless communities enables destructive behavior. He advocated for distinguishing between local residents and transients from other areas, noting that homeless people account for disproportionate emergency calls (20-50% vs. less than 1% of population). He argued true compassion requires making it uncomfortable for people not to change behavior, citing successes only when people become sober and productive.
public_comment.topic: Homelessness, compassion, and fairness in law enforcement response

unanswered: Pamela Holder asked for data and description of what conduct has taken place that would constitute enforcement and how big the loitering/homeless issue actually is in Brevard, and how to determine if someone is in the social district. Chief Wentzell deferred provision of data to a later date.
Gary Daniel asked whether the list of city-owned properties subject to trespassing ordinance is complete, citing parklets and public alleyways. Chief Wentzell confirmed the list may be incomplete.

Erin Baker asked whether there would be additional reporting requirements at the public safety committee level beyond annual crime statistics to catch potential overpolicing of loitering ordinance. No firm commitment made to specific reporting frequency.

Lauren Wise asked for clarification on how state general statutes versus local ordinances work, specifically whether loitering is addressed at state level. Chief Wentzell explained loitering alone is not a state crime except on state highways.

disagreements.issue: Parks and Recreation capital fund structure: single project-specific fund vs. umbrella fund with multiple projects

positions.position: Advocated for comprehensive Parks and Recreation umbrella fund with sports complex as earmarked project, to ensure coordinated planning across all three recreation facilities (sports complex, Franklin Park, Silverstein), establish unified standards, and enable long-term capital improvement planning

Initially recommended separate sports complex capital project fund to maintain specificity and prevent funds from being diverted to other purposes; noted preference for clear fund names to track distinct capital projects
Supported Luby's initial approach, noting that the $46,000 and $11,000 were specifically targeted amounts based on engineering plan by McAdams for specific use

Agreed with spirit of Weidel's concerns about comprehensive planning but acknowledged trade-off: specific funds establish priority but limit flexibility for future needs and contingency money; suggested decision needed at project completion about leftover funds
Recalled earlier conversation supporting comprehensive recreational fund concept with sports complex as initial priority; supported Weidel's position

disagreements.issue: COLA adjustment: 2.7% vs. 3% for employee salary increase

positions.position: Recommended 3% option, noting $28,000 savings from tipper cart removal nearly equals cost to bump from 2.7% to 3%; argued 3% gets closer to matching CPI (reported 4.8-5%)
Concerned about losing merit raise opportunities; suggested 2.8% or 2.9% to preserve merit compensation pool funding
Supported 3% as important signal to staff that their work is valued; cited need to maintain competitive salaries to retain employees
Supported 3% citing new CPI report showing 4.2% inflation, immediate impact on salary ranges for open positions, and need for competitiveness
Acknowledged merit raises important but agreed $28,000 insufficient for effective merit pool; supported using money for COLA but emphasized merit raises should not be lost sight of

disagreements.issue: Railroad Avenue Extension project in Comprehensive Transportation Plan

positions.position: Strongly opposed Railroad Avenue Extension (Project 17), raised alarm bells in TAC meeting; made motion to remove (failed); advocated for replacement with Wilson Road project as workable alternative; stated Railroad Avenue is not a bypass despite some calling it that
Responded that project on plan but acknowledged alternatives; supported Wilson Road project as replacement after discussion
Agreed with Wise; noted project discussed for 20 years, bubbled up 10-12 years ago with public input causing shelving; supported removal and Wilson Road replacement

disagreements.issue: Legislative request addition for $300,000 bathroom facilities at Silverstein Park

Argued legislative requests are separate from budget, not part of current budget vote; suggested postponing discussion and potentially reopening entire legislative request in future agenda rather than singular project
Advised motion to add legislative request item to agenda would require amending agenda
Voted down (2 ayes, 3 nays) motion to amend agenda to add legislative request discussion
